149: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS (HOW_IT_WORKS): CHANGELOG OUTPUT MODES
150: 
151: ### Global Component Changelog
152: 
153: A global entry is written to `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`. `{component}` is a lowercase kebab-case segment matching `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, or `{hub}/{link}` when the folder is a hub, with each segment matching that pattern. Reject an ambiguous hint rather than emit a guessed or underscore-bearing directory. The `v{VERSION}.md` filename is an exact version contract and is never slug-normalized.
154: 
155: | Bump | Calculation | Source trigger intent |
156: | --- | --- | --- |
157: | `major` | `{MAJOR+1}.0.0.0` | Breaking, overhaul, rewrite, migration, platform version jump |
158: | `minor` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR+1}.0.0` | Significant new feature or subsystem addition |
159: | `patch` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH+1}.0` | Incremental improvement, bug fix, refactor, docs, cleanup |
160: | `build` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}.{BUILD+1}` | Hotfix, typo, same-day build on an already-published version |
161: 
162: Auto detection takes the explicit `--bump` flag first, then change-type keywords in the `spec.md` title and purpose, then conventional commit prefixes. With no clear signal it defaults to `patch`. If the calculated file already exists, increment the build segment until the path is unique.
163: 
164: ### Packet-Local Nested Changelog
165: 
166: Packet-local changelogs use no global component folder and no four-part version. A root spec folder writes to `changelog/changelog-<packet>-root.md`, and a phase child writes to `../changelog/changelog-<packet>-<phase-folder>.md`. `<packet>` and `<phase-folder>` are validated kebab-case segments. Keep the fixed `changelog-` prefix and `-root.md` suffix, and reject a slug that cannot be resolved without collision.
167: 
168: Nested mode writes through the spec-kit generator, whose templates are `.skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/templates/changelog/root.md` and `phase.md` beside it:
169: 
170: ```bash
171: node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/dist/spec-folder/nested-changelog.js <spec-folder> --write
172: ```
173:

176: ## 5. CHANGELOG FORMAT CONTRACT
177: 
178: Read `assets/changelog-template.md` before generating global content. It owns the compact and expanded shapes (section 2), what to leave out and the say-it-once rule (section 3), voice and length (section 4) and format selection (section 5). Every entry must be able to sit beside the canonical exemplar, `.skilled/changelog/skilled/v4.0.0.0.md`, without looking out of place.
179: 
180: The contract in one pass:
181: 
182: 1. Frontmatter first, then an optional editorial title H1, then the summary narrative. No version header, backlink or version-date line.
183: 2. Compact under 10 reader-visible changes when the release is neither major nor breaking: summary, `## What's New at a Glance` and `## Upgrade`, with `## Why This Release` only when the summary does not say why.
184: 3. Expanded for 10 or more changes, a major bump or any breaking change: opening narrative, `## Why This Release`, `## What's New at a Glance`, topical H2 sections with benefit-led H4 items and `## Upgrade Notes`.
185: 4. A spec-folder blockquote, `> Spec folder: `{path}` (Level {N})`, when the release has a spec folder.
186: 5. Content chosen by reader impact and each fact said once. No file, test or schema tables unless the numbers are the story.
187: 
188: When a source such as an older command snippet conflicts with the template, follow the template, write the narrative format and record the mismatch rather than inventing a hybrid.
189: 
190: ### Frontmatter Contract
191: 
192: A global entry must be as findable as a spec document, so its frontmatter block carries these five keys, in this order:
193: 
194: | Key | Value |
195: | --- | --- |
196: | `title` | `<component> v<version>, <editorial title>`, or `<component> v<version>` when the entry has no editorial title. A Skilled release entry uses its H1, or `Skilled v<version>` |
197: | `description` | One or two plain sentences, 250 characters at most, saying what the release changed |
198: | `trigger_phrases` | The identity phrases first, then one or two topic phrases |
199: | `importance_tier` | `"normal"` |
200: | `contextType` | `"general"` |
201: 
202: Identity phrases name the entry the way a reader asks for it. A skill entry declares `<component> v<version>` and `<component> <version>`, where `<component>` is the `name:` in the `SKILL.md` of the folder that holds the entry's changelog folder, never a `{hub}/{link}` target. The deep-loop runtime has no `SKILL.md` and is `deep-loop-runtime`. A Skilled release entry declares `v<version> release notes` and `skilled v<version>`. A topic phrase is 2 to 6 words from the entry's own text that name what changed. It carries no version number and never fits any release the way "bug fixes" would. A component entry may keep a `version:` key after the five.
203: 
204: Packet-local entries take their block from the spec-kit nested templates, and the nested generator derives their identity phrase from the output path.

208: ## 6. TOPOLOGY AND TARGET RESOLUTION
209: 
210: ### Mode Detection
211: 
212: For a spec folder, read `implementation-summary.md` first and `spec.md` for the title, purpose and level. Read `tasks.md` only to confirm what shipped. Then pick the output mode:
213: 
214: 1. `--nested` present: nested mode.
215: 2. The folder is a phase child, has direct child phase folders or already has `changelog/`: nested mode.
216: 3. Otherwise: global mode.
217: 
218: A component hint or git history source is always global mode, built from recent commits and the files they touched.
219: 
220: ### Global Component Discovery
221: 
222: Discover component folders from the repository at run time with `ls -d .skilled/changelog/*/ 2>/dev/null | sort`, never from a hardcoded table. Then resolve:
223: 
224: 1. Each folder is a plain component name, such as `sk-doc` or `system-spec-kit`, with no numeric prefix. One folder is not a skill: `skilled` is the framework release line, with one entry per Skilled release.
225: 2. Match changed paths against folder names by whole path segment, never by substring.
226: 3. Match `.skilled/skills/{name}/**` to the folder named `{name}`, and `.skilled/commands/**` or `.skilled/agents/**` to the folder that owns them.
227: 4. Resolve a hub to one of its links, never to the hub folder. A hub is a real folder other than `skilled`, such as `sk-doc` or `sk-code`, holding one link per member packet plus `parent`, the hub's own changelog. `ls -l .skilled/changelog/{hub}/` lists them. A path under `.skilled/skills/{hub}/{packet}/` resolves to the link whose target is `{packet}/changelog`. Any other path under the hub, and a hint that names the hub, resolve to `{hub}/parent`. A hint that names a member by its link, its packet folder or `{hub}/{link}` resolves to that link.
228: 5. Match `component_hint` against folder names exactly.
229: 6. Use spec path segments as a tiebreaker.
230: 7. Resolve to `skilled` only when `component_hint` names it. A changed path never selects it, because the operator chooses a framework release.
231: 8. If nothing matches, do not invent or default a folder. Pause and ask which component the changelog belongs to.
232: 
233: Then choose the target:
234: 
235: 1. A component with more than 60 percent of the changed files is primary.
236: 2. With several roughly equal components, pick the primary by file count and list the rest as secondary.
237: 3. Verify the target folder exists before writing, and never create a missing one.

241: ## 7. CREATION WORKFLOW
242: 
243: Complete these seven steps in order. The command YAMLs number the same workflow as eight steps, because they run the optional GitHub release as its own step 7.
244: 
245: Before writing, validate each authored component, packet or phase slug. Exact version filenames and frozen changelog paths stay exempt.
246: 
247: ```bash
248: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/check_authored_name_kebab.py <component-or-phase-slug>
249: ```
250: 
251: 1. **Analyze context.** Resolve the source type and read the source (section 6). Compile `work_context`: what changed for the reader, the change type, the level and the source.
252: 2. **Resolve output target.** Nested mode: run the nested generator with `--json`, read the root or phase template and take the output path from it. Global mode: discover the folders, match paths and hints (section 6), choose the primary component, list secondary ones and verify `.skilled/changelog/{resolved_folder}/` exists.
253: 3. **Determine version.** Nested mode skips this. Global mode lists the `v*.md` entries in the target folder and in its generation folders (`v1+/`, `v2+/` and so on), lists the version entries on the upstream branch with `git ls-tree` (the branch's upstream, else `origin/main`), takes the highest of the local and upstream `vX.Y.Z.B` versions, chooses the bump (section 4) and calculates the next version, incrementing the build segment while the file exists locally or upstream, because two branches numbering from their own checkout pick the same version and collide at merge. Without a reachable upstream it numbers locally and says so in the report.
254: 4. **Generate content.** Read `assets/changelog-template.md`, or the spec-kit nested template in nested mode. In global mode:
255:    - Write the frontmatter block per the Frontmatter Contract in section 5.
256:    - Choose the content before writing it (template section 3). List what changed, keep what the reader would notice, act on or decide differently about, merge items with the same effect and drop the housekeeping.
257:    - Select compact or expanded from the changes that survive (template section 5).
258:    - Write each section to its one job, so a fact appears once: themes in the opening, the gap in Why This Release, one payoff line per theme at a glance, the detail in the H4 items and only actions in the upgrade notes.
259:    - Lead with why the release matters, and add a table only when its numbers are the story.
260: 5. **Validate quality.** Run the section 9 checks on the draft. Confirm the version is strictly greater than the latest one, no file exists at the target and every path the entry names exists. Apply the cut test (template section 3), fix what is safe and revalidate.
261: 6. **Write the file.** Nested mode: run `node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/dist/spec-folder/nested-changelog.js {spec_folder} --write` and verify the output path. Global mode: write `.skilled/changelog/{primary_component}/v{next_version}.md`, read back its first lines, then set `next_version` in every version carrier the component's skill root already has (`SKILL.md`, `description.json`, `hub-router.json` and `mode-registry.json`, never `README.md` or a hub `ROUTER.md`, whose versions are each document's own) and, for a hub, run `node .skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/parent-skill-check.cjs` on the hub and stop on a non-zero exit. Report secondary components as candidates rather than writing extra files.
262: 7. **Report and preserve context.** Report the path, component, version, bump type, summary, section count and files tracked. A spec-folder source can preserve context through the normal memory save workflow. Do not claim completion before the written file is verified.
263: 
264: Pause when confidence drops below 40 percent, component resolution stays ambiguous, the calculated version looks wrong or a required section would be empty.

268: ## 8. NOTATION AND FORMAT RULES
269: 
270: The voice, structure, omission and length rules live in `assets/changelog-template.md` sections 3 and 4. The non-negotiables are:
271: 
272: 1. Write for a smart person who is not a developer, and lead with why the release matters.
273: 2. Keep what the reader would notice or act on. Drop file inventories, test counts, internal labels, process detail and follow-on housekeeping, and compress reverted work to one story sentence or nothing.
274: 3. Say each fact once, in the section whose job it is.
275: 4. Bold lead-in sentences on glance bullets, H4 item headings of 2-7 words (10 at most), an ` ` line before every H2 (the opening, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance and every later section), nothing between H4 items, no `---` rule in the body and inline `**Breaking:**` markers.
276: 5. No Oxford commas, em dashes or semicolons, per the Human Voice Rules.
277: 
278: ### Release Notes
279: 
280: For GitHub release notes, use the changelog content with any YAML frontmatter and the editorial title H1 removed, keeping its spacing, then append an ` ` line and the pointer:
281: 
282: ```text
283:  
284: 
285: Full changelog: `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`
286: ```
287: 
288: The command YAMLs own the release itself, as `step_7_publish_release`, and run it only when `publish_release` is explicitly true and the component is `skilled`, the framework release line. Any other component skips the release, because component versions share the `vX.X.X.X` shape with release tags and a component version must never become one. The tag is `v{next_version}`, and the release title is the tag followed by the entry's editorial title, the H1 without its leading version. The step checks for a tag collision and an authenticated `gh`, then runs `git tag -a`, `git push origin {release_tag}` and `gh release create {release_tag} --title {release_title} --notes-file {notes_file}`, which publishes at once with no draft stage. `:confirm` shows the exact commands and runs them only after approval. A packet-local changelog never releases, because it has no repo-wide version to tag.

225: 2. Match changed paths against folder names by whole path segment, never by substring.
226: 3. Match `.skilled/skills/{name}/**` to the folder named `{name}`, and `.skilled/commands/**` or `.skilled/agents/**` to the folder that owns them.
227: 4. Resolve a hub to one of its links, never to the hub folder. A hub is a real folder other than `skilled`, such as `sk-doc` or `sk-code`, holding one link per member packet plus `parent`, the hub's own changelog. `ls -l .skilled/changelog/{hub}/` lists them. A path under `.skilled/skills/{hub}/{packet}/` resolves to the link whose target is `{packet}/changelog`. Any other path under the hub, and a hint that names the hub, resolve to `{hub}/parent`. 228: 5. Match `component_hint` against folder names exactly.
229: 6. Use spec path segments as a tiebreaker.
230: 7. Resolve to `skilled` only when `component_hint` names it. A changed path never selects it, because the operator chooses a framework release.
231: 8. If nothing matches, do not invent or default a folder. Pause and ask which component the changelog belongs to.
232: 
233: Then choose the target:
234: 
235: 1. A component with more than 60 percent of the changed files is primary.
236: 2. With several roughly equal components, pick the primary by file count and list the rest as secondary.
237: 3. Verify the target folder exists before writing, and never create a missing one.

241: ## 7. CREATION WORKFLOW
242: 
243: Complete these seven steps in order. The command YAMLs number the same workflow as eight steps, because they run the optional GitHub release as its own step 7.
244: 
245: Before writing, validate each authored component, packet or phase slug. Exact version filenames and frozen changelog paths stay exempt.
246: 
247: ```bash
248: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/check_authored_name_kebab.py <component-or-phase-slug>
249: ```
250: 
251: 1. **Analyze context.** Resolve the source type and read the source (section 6). Compile `work_context`: what changed for the reader, the change type, the level and the source.
252: 2. **Resolve output target.** Nested mode: run the nested generator with `--json`, read the root or phase template and take the output path from it. Global mode: discover the folders, match paths and hints (section 6), choose the primary component, list secondary ones and verify `.skilled/changelog/{resolved_folder}/` exists.
253: 3. **Determine version.** Nested mode skips this. Global mode lists the `v*.md` entries in the target folder and in its generation folders (`v1+/`, `v2+/` and so on), lists the version entries on the upstream branch with `git ls-tree` (the branch's upstream, else `origin/main`), takes the highest of the local and upstream `vX.Y.Z.B` versions, chooses the bump (section 4) and calculates the next version, incrementing the build segment while the file exists locally or upstream, because two branches numbering from their own checkout pick the same version and collide at merge. Without a reachable upstream it numbers locally and says so in the report.
254: 4. **Generate content.** Read `assets/changelog-template.md`, or the spec-kit nested template in nested mode. In global mode:
255:    - Write the frontmatter block per the Frontmatter Contract in section 5.
256:    - Choose the content before writing it (template section 3). List what changed, keep what the reader would notice, act on or decide differently about, merge items with the same effect and drop the housekeeping.
257:    - Select compact or expanded from the changes that survive (template section 5).
258:    - Write each section to its one job, so a fact appears once: themes in the opening, the gap in Why This Release, one payoff line per theme at a glance, the detail in the H4 items and only actions in the upgrade notes.
259:    - Lead with why the release matters, and add a table only when its numbers are the story.
260: 5. **Validate quality.** Run the section 9 checks on the draft. Confirm the version is strictly greater than the latest one, no file exists at the target and every path the entry names exists. Apply the cut test (template section 3), fix what is safe and revalidate.
261: 6. **Write the file.** Nested mode: run `node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/dist/spec-folder/nested-changelog.js {spec_folder} --write` and verify the output path. Global mode: write `.skilled/changelog/{primary_component}/v{next_version}.md`, read back its first lines, then set `next_version` in every version carrier the component's skill root already has (`SKILL.md`, `description.json`, `hub-router.json` and `mode-registry.json`, never `README.md` or a hub `ROUTER.md`, whose versions are each document's own) and, for a hub, run `node .skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/parent-skill-check.cjs` on the hub and stop on a non-zero exit. Report secondary components as candidates rather than writing extra files.
262: 7. **Report and preserve context.** Report the path, component, version, bump type, summary, section count and files tracked. A spec-folder source can preserve context through the normal memory save workflow. Do not claim completion before the written file is verified.
263: 
264: Pause when confidence drops below 40 percent, component resolution stays ambiguous, the calculated version looks wrong or a required section would be empty.

268: ## 8. NOTATION AND FORMAT RULES
269: 
270: The voice, structure, omission and length rules live in `assets/changelog-template.md` sections 3 and 4. The non-negotiables are:
271: 
272: 1. Write for a smart person who is not a developer, and lead with why the release matters.
273: 2. Keep what the reader would notice or act on. Drop file inventories, test counts, internal labels, process detail and follow-on housekeeping, and compress reverted work to one story sentence or nothing.
274: 3. Say each fact once, in the section whose job it is.
275: 4. Bold lead-in sentences on glance bullets, H4 item headings of 2-7 words (10 at most), an ` ` line before every H2 (the opening, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance and every later section), nothing between H4 items, no `---` rule in the body and inline `**Breaking:**` markers.
276: 5. No Oxford commas, em dashes or semicolons, per the Human Voice Rules.

280: For GitHub release notes, use the changelog content with any YAML frontmatter and the editorial title H1 removed, keeping its spacing, then append an ` ` line and the pointer:

245: ## 9. VALIDATION
246:

249: Global changelog checks:

292: ## 10. RULES
293: 
294: ### ✅ ALWAYS
295: 
296: 1. Follow the seven-step workflow in order.
297: 2. Read `assets/changelog-template.md` before generating global content.
298: 3. Discover global component folders from `.skilled/changelog/` at run time, and resolve to an existing one before writing.
299: 4. Keep global versions four-part and strictly sequential. Extending an untagged `skilled` release keeps its version.
300: 5. Choose content by reader impact and say each fact once.
301: 6. Refuse `--nested` and route a spec-folder source to a global component entry.
302: 7. List secondary affected components.
303: 8. Verify the written file before claiming completion.
304: 9. Keep this packet self-contained, with the advisor identity at the `sk-doc` hub root.

307: 
308: 1. Add a packet-local `graph-metadata.json`.

311: 4. Write an entry with an empty summary or an empty required section.

149: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS (HOW_IT_WORKS): CHANGELOG OUTPUT MODES
150: 
151: ### Global Component Changelog
152: 
153: A global entry is written to `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`. `{component}` is a lowercase kebab-case segment matching `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, or `{hub}/{link}` when the folder is a hub, with each segment matching that pattern. Reject an ambiguous hint rather than emit a guessed or underscore-bearing directory. The `v{VERSION}.md` filename is an exact version contract and is never slug-normalized.
154: 
155: | Bump | Calculation | Source trigger intent |
156: | --- | --- | --- |
157: | `major` | `{MAJOR+1}.0.0.0` | Breaking, overhaul, rewrite, migration, platform version jump |
158: | `minor` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR+1}.0.0` | Significant new feature or subsystem addition |
159: | `patch` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH+1}.0` | Incremental improvement, bug fix, refactor, docs, cleanup |
160: | `build` | `{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}.{BUILD+1}` | Hotfix, typo, same-day build on an already-published version |
161: 
162: Auto detection takes the explicit `--bump` flag first, then change-type keywords in the `spec.md` title and purpose, then conventional commit prefixes. With no clear signal it defaults to `patch`. If the calculated file already exists, increment the build segment until the path is unique.

164: ### Packet-Local Nested Changelog
165: 
166: Packet-local changelogs use no global component folder and no four-part version. A root spec folder writes to `changelog/changelog-<packet>-root.md`, and a phase child writes to `../changelog/changelog-<packet>-<phase-folder>.md`. `<packet>` and `<phase-folder>` are validated kebab-case segments. Keep the fixed `changelog-` prefix and `-root.md` suffix, and reject a slug that cannot be resolved without collision.

169: 
170: ```bash

172: ```

176: ## 5. CHANGELOG FORMAT CONTRACT
177:

It owns the compact and expanded shapes (section 2), what to leave out and the say-it-once rule (section 3), voice and length (section 4) and format selection (section 5). 208: ## 6. TOPOLOGY AND TARGET RESOLUTION
209: 
210: ### Mode Detection
211: 
212: For a spec folder, read `implementation-summary.md` first and `spec.md` for the title, purpose and level. Read `tasks.md` only to confirm what shipped. Then pick the output mode:
213: 
214: 1. `--nested` present: nested mode.
215: 2. The folder is a phase child, has direct child phase folders or already has `changelog/`: nested mode.
216: 3. Otherwise: global mode.

220: ### Global Component Discovery
221: 
222: Discover component folders from the repository at run time with `ls -d .skilled/changelog/*/ 2>/dev/null | sort`, never from a hardcoded table. Then resolve:
223: 
224: 1. Each folder is a plain component name, such as `sk-doc` or `system-spec-kit`, with no numeric prefix. One folder is not a skill: `skilled` is the framework release line, with one entry per Skilled release.

257:    - Select compact or expanded from the changes that survive (template section 5).

268: ## 8. NOTATION AND FORMAT RULES
269: 
270: The voice, structure, omission and length rules live in `assets/changelog-template.md` sections 3 and 4. The non-negotiables are:
271: 
272: 1. Write for a smart person who is not a developer, and lead with why the release matters.
273: 2. Keep what the reader would notice or act on. Drop file inventories, test counts, internal labels, process detail and follow-on housekeeping, and compress reverted work to one story sentence or nothing.
274: 3. Say each fact once, in the section whose job it is.
275: 4. Bold lead-in sentences on glance bullets, H4 item headings of 2-7 words (10 at most), an ` ` line before every H2 (the opening, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance and every later section), nothing between H4 items, no `---` rule in the body and inline `**Breaking:**` markers.
276: 5. No Oxford commas, em dashes or semicolons, per the Human Voice Rules.

278: ### Release Notes
279: 
280: For GitHub release notes, use the changelog content with any YAML frontmatter and the editorial title H1 removed, keeping its spacing, then append an ` ` line and the pointer:
281: 
282: ```text
283:  
284: 
285: Full changelog: `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`
286: ```
287: 
288: The command YAMLs own the release itself, as `step_7_publish_release`, and run it only when `publish_release` is explicitly true and the component is `skilled`, the framework release line. Any other component skips the release, because component versions share the `vX.X.X.X` shape with release tags and a component version must never become one. The tag is `v{next_version}`, and the release title is the tag followed by the entry's editorial title, the H1 without its leading version. The step checks for a tag collision and an authenticated `gh`, then runs `git tag -a`, `git push origin {release_tag}` and `gh release create {release_tag} --title {release_title} --notes-file {notes_file}`, which publishes at once with no draft stage. `:confirm` shows the exact commands and runs them only after approval. A packet-local changelog never releases, because it has no repo-wide version to tag.

15: # Changelog & Release Notes Templates - Format Reference
16: 
17: Two narrative formats for global component changelogs and their GitHub release notes. Every rule below serves one goal: the reader learns what changed for them and why, in the fewest words that still carry the connection.
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### The Canonical Exemplar
22: 
23: `.skilled/changelog/skilled/v4.0.0.0.md` is the house style, so read it before writing. It shows the opening narrative, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance, topical H2 sections with benefit-led H4 items, inline Breaking markers and Upgrade Notes. Copy its voice and shape, not its length: it records a major release, and most releases need a fraction of it. Older entries in the same folders predate this style, so do not copy them. When this template and the exemplar disagree on shape, the exemplar wins and the discrepancy is recorded.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: The `/create:changelog` workflow reads this template at step 4. Section 5 picks the format. Packet-local changelogs are deprecated and no longer written (section 7).
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. THE TWO TIERS
32: 
33: Every entry opens with the frontmatter block that SKILL.md section 5 defines. An editorial title H1 may follow it, and then the prose starts with the summary narrative. The retired machine header (a bare version title, a backlink, a version-date line) stays gone.
34: 
35: ### Compact Format (under 10 changes, non-breaking)
36: 
37: ```markdown
38: ---
39: title: "{component} v{VERSION}"
40: description: "{What the release changed, in one or two plain sentences of 250 characters at most.}"
41: trigger_phrases:
42:   - "{component} v{VERSION}"
43:   - "{component} {VERSION}"
44:   - "{Topic phrase: 2-6 words from this entry that name what changed}"
45: importance_tier: "normal"
46: contextType: "general"
47: ---
48: 
49: {Summary: 1-3 sentences on what the release does for the reader and why it matters.}
50: 
51: > Spec folder: `{path}` (Level {N})
52: 
53:  
54: 
55: ## What's New at a Glance
56: 
57: - **{The change, as a short sentence.}** {One plain sentence that adds what the bold one does not say.}
58: 
59:  
60: 
61: ## Upgrade
62: 
63: {The action the reader must take, or "No migration required."}
64: ```
65: 
66: Include the spec-folder line only when the release has a spec folder. Add a `## Why This Release` section of 2-4 sentences after the summary only when the summary does not already say why, with an ` ` line before it like every other H2.
67: 
68: ### Expanded Format (10+ changes, major or breaking)
69: 
70: ```markdown
71: {The same frontmatter block as the compact format.}
72: 
73: {Opening narrative: 1-5 paragraphs in plain prose, one per theme, no headers.}
74: 
75: > Spec folder: `{path}` (Level {N})
76: 
77:  
78: 
79: ## Why This Release
80: 
81: {Why the release exists: the gap it closes or the gain it buys, in one to three short paragraphs or bold lead-in gain bullets.}
82: 
83:  
84: 
85: ## What's New at a Glance
86: 
87: - **{The theme, as a short sentence.}** {One plain sentence that adds what the bold one does not say.}
88: 
89:  
90: 
91: ## {Topical Domain}
92: 
93: {Optional 1-2 sentence introduction.}
94: 
95: #### {Benefit-led heading, usually 2-7 words}
96: 
97: {One or two paragraphs for most items, seven at most: what was broken, what changed and why it matters. Start where the glance bullet stopped.}
98: 
99: #### {Next heading}
100: 
101: **Breaking:** {What breaks and exactly what to do about it.}
102: 
103:  
104: 
105: ## Upgrade Notes
106: 
107: - **Adopt.** {Renames and new things to start using.}
108: - **Repoint.** {Moved paths and surfaces that changed address.}
109: - **Drop.** {Removed things and what replaces them.}
110: ```
111: 
112: Include the spec-folder line only when the release has a spec folder.
113: 
114: **Field guidelines**:
115: 
116: - **`{Topical Domain}` (H2).** Name the section for the domain it changes, the way the exemplar names `Spec Kit` and `Safer Git`, never for a change type such as `New Features` or `Bug Fixes`. Most releases need one to five domains. A release the exemplar's size may need more when each one earns its section.
117: - **`{Benefit-led heading}` (H4).** 2-7 words for most headings and 10 at most, stating the gain or the fact. Good: `Specs Move to the Top Level`. Bad: `Improved validation logic`, a numbered item or a sentence-length title.
118: - **Separators.** An ` ` line, a forced blank line, goes before every H2: between the opening and Why This Release, between Why This Release and What's New at a Glance, and between every later section. Nothing separates the H4 items inside one H2, and no `---` rule appears anywhere in the entry body.
119: - **Upgrade Notes.** Use the Adopt, Repoint and Drop lead-ins only when the release has all three kinds of work. Otherwise write plain bullets or a short paragraph, and "No upgrade needed." when there is nothing to do.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 3. WHAT TO LEAVE OUT
124: 
125: What goes in decides the length more than the wording does, so choose the content before writing any of it. Every item dropped stays findable in the spec packet.
126: 
127: ### Choose by Reader Impact
128: 
129: List every change the source records. Keep an item only when the reader would notice it, act on it or decide differently because of it. Merge items that have the same effect for the reader, and lead with the one that matters most. A task list is evidence of what shipped, not an outline: ten tasks that produced one visible change make one bullet.
130: 
131: ### Keep
132: 
133: - User-visible behavior changes, stated as before and after.
134: - Breaking changes and the exact migration step.
135: - Anything the reader must do, adopt, repoint or stop using.
136: - Honest corrections of a claim a previous release got wrong.
137: - Numbers that are the claim itself, such as a measured cost or a limit the reader must stay under.
138: 
139: ### Drop by Default
140: 
141: - File inventories and Files Changed tables.
142: - Test counts, test tables and new test or playbook scenarios.
143: - Schema internals, index churn and machinery names the reader never touches.
144: - Internal labels such as task or requirement IDs, scenario IDs and packet or phase numbers. The spec-folder line is the one pointer an entry needs.
145: - How the work was done: review rounds, models, agents and research phases, unless it changes how far the reader can trust the result.
146: - Follow-on housekeeping: docs brought in line with the change, regenerated copies, rebuilt indexes and refreshed metadata or versions.
147: - Small fixes with no visible effect. Fold several into one sentence, or leave them out.
148: - Work tried and reverted during the cycle. It gets one story sentence at most, written into the narrative: what was tried and that it left before release. The exemplar's model is "An alignment mode was built during the cycle and removed before release, and the removal took `/deep:command-benchmark` and the conformance benchmark family with it."
149: 
150: ### Say Each Fact Once
151: 
152: Each section has one job, and a fact lives in the section whose job it is.
153: 
154: | Section | Its job | Not its job |
155: |---|---|---|
156: | Summary or opening | What the release does, told at the level of themes | Fix-by-fix detail and the numbers behind it |
157: | Why This Release | The gap the release closes or the gain it buys | The list of changes, which the glance section carries |
158: | What's New at a Glance | One line per theme, stating the payoff | The full mechanism or a sentence that restates the bold one |
159: | Topical H4 items | The detail: before, mechanism and after | The glance bullet's sentence, said again |
160: | Upgrade Notes | The actions, one line each | Why the change was made |
161: 
162: When a sentence would repeat an earlier one, cut it or replace it with something the reader does not know yet. In a compact entry, each glance bullet must add something the summary did not say.
163: 
164: ### When a Table Earns Its Place
165: 
166: A table appears only when the numbers are the claim. The exemplar carries one in six hundred lines, the measured cached-input cost per model, because the dollar difference was the finding. A table that restates prose, lists files or counts tests does not earn its place, and most entries carry none.
167: 
168: ### The Cut Test
169: 
170: Before writing the file, ask of each sentence whether the reader would miss it. Cut the ones they would not. Then check the joints: concise is not compressed, so keep the "because" and the before-and-after that make a change make sense, and restore the noun when a cut leaves a "this" with nothing to point at.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 4. WRITING STYLE RULES
175: 
176: These rules apply to changelog files and GitHub release notes. The Human Voice Rules are the authority on banned patterns, and the validator enforces both.
177: 
178: ### Voice
179: 
180: - Write for a smart person who is not a developer.
181: - Lead with why the release matters, never with technical stats.
182: - Explain each change as what was broken, what changed and why it matters.
183: - One idea per sentence, active voice, no hedging.
184: - Define a technical term on first use, such as "BM25 (exact word matching)".
185: - Name an identifier (a skill, a path or a command) only where the reader acts on it, the way the exemplar names `mode-registry.json` where it explains dispatch.
186: - No Oxford commas, em dashes or semicolons, per `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md`.
187: 
188: ### Structure
189: 
190: - Bold lead-in bullets for lists of gains or upgrade steps.
191: - H4 (`####`) for item headings, never H3. No `**Problem:**` or `**Fix:**` labels.
192: - Inline `**Breaking:**` markers where the break is described, not a separate section.
193: - No metrics soup: never pack many numbers into one sentence.
194: 
195: ### Length
196: 
197: | Element | Usually | Ceiling |
198: |---|---|---|
199: | Summary paragraph | 1-2 sentences | 3 sentences |
200: | Expanded opening narrative | 1-3 paragraphs | 5 paragraphs |
201: | Why This Release | 1-2 short paragraphs | 3 short paragraphs or 4 sentences, gain bullets allowed |
202: | What's New at a Glance | 3-6 bullets compact, 5-9 expanded | 12 bullets, one line each |
203: | Glance bullet | A bold sentence and one plain sentence | A bold sentence and three plain sentences |
204: | H4 item narrative | 1-2 paragraphs | 7 paragraphs |
205: | H4 heading | 2-7 words | 10 words |
206: | Compact file total | 10-25 lines of prose | 40 lines of prose |
207: 
208: Validation checks the ceilings, and each one sits at or above what the exemplar does, so the exemplar passes every check it teaches. The usual column is the target. A release with one fix reads short.
209: 
210: ---
211: 
212: ## 5. FORMAT SELECTION GUIDE
213: 
214: | Release Type | Format | When to Use |
215: |---|---|---|
216: | Hotfix (1-3 changes) | Compact | Quick bug fix, typo correction |
217: | Feature release (4-9 changes) | Compact | New feature, small refactor |
218: | Major release (10+ changes) | Expanded | Overhaul, multi-part work |
219: | Breaking change | Expanded | Any release requiring migration, regardless of count |
220: 
221: Count the changes that survive section 3, not the tasks behind them.
222: 
223: ```text
224: Count the changes in the release.
225: ├─> < 10 changes AND not major AND not breaking  → Compact format
226: ├─> >= 10 changes OR major bump                  → Expanded format
227: └─> Any breaking change                          → Expanded format
228: ```
229: 
230: ---
231: 
232: ## 6. GITHUB RELEASE NOTES FORMAT
233: 
234: The release body is the changelog content with any YAML frontmatter and the editorial title H1 removed, because GitHub shows the release title on its own. It keeps the entry's spacing, an ` ` line before every H2 and nothing between H4 items. The release step in the command YAMLs strips both before it runs `gh release create`, then appends an ` ` line and the pointer:
235: 
236: ```text
237:  
238: 
239: Full changelog: `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`
240: ```
241: 
242: The release title is the tag, an em dash and the editorial title, `v{VERSION} — {Editorial Title}`, and the tag is annotated with the message `v{VERSION}: {Editorial Title}`.
243: 
244: ---
245: 
246: ## 7. NESTED PACKET-LOCAL CHANGELOGS (DEPRECATED)
247: 
248: Spec folders no longer get changelogs, so no workflow writes a new file under `specs/**/changelog/`. A change recorded in a spec folder goes into a global entry for the component it touched, written from this template.
249: 
250: Existing `changelog-<packet>-root.md` and `changelog-<packet>-<phase-folder>.md` files stay and still validate. The spec-kit nested generator remains only to render them and prints a deprecation notice. Do not reuse this template for them.
251: 
252: ---
253: 
254: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES

14: 
15: # Changelog & Release Notes Templates - Format Reference
16: 
17: Two narrative formats for global component changelogs and their GitHub release notes. Every rule below serves one goal: the reader learns what changed for them and why, in the fewest words that still carry the connection.
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### The Canonical Exemplar
22: 
23: `.skilled/changelog/skilled/v4.0.0.0.md` is the house style, so read it before writing. It shows the opening narrative, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance, topical H2 sections with benefit-led H4 items, inline Breaking markers and Upgrade Notes. Copy its voice and shape, not its length: it records a major release, and most releases need a fraction of it. Older entries in the same folders predate this style, so do not copy them. When this template and the exemplar disagree on shape, the exemplar wins and the discrepancy is recorded.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: The `/create:changelog` workflow reads this template at step 4. Section 5 picks the format. Packet-local changelogs are deprecated and no longer written (section 7).
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. THE TWO TIERS
32: 
33: Every entry opens with the frontmatter block that SKILL.md section 5 defines. An editorial title H1 may follow it, and then the prose starts with the summary narrative. The retired machine header (a bare version title, a backlink, a version-date line) stays gone.
34: 
35: ### Compact Format (under 10 changes, non-breaking)
36: 
37: ```markdown
38: ---
39: title: "{component} v{VERSION}"
40: description: "{What the release changed, in one or two plain sentences of 250 characters at most.}"
41: trigger_phrases:
42:   - "{component} v{VERSION}"
43:   - "{component} {VERSION}"
44:   - "{Topic phrase: 2-6 words from this entry that name what changed}"
45: importance_tier: "normal"
46: contextType: "general"
47: ---
48: 
49: {Summary: 1-3 sentences on what the release does for the reader and why it matters.}
50: 
51: > Spec folder: `{path}` (Level {N})
52: 
53:  
54: 
55: ## What's New at a Glance
56: 
57: - **{The change, as a short sentence.}** {One plain sentence that adds what the bold one does not say.}
58: 
59:  
60: 
61: ## Upgrade
62: 
63: {The action the reader must take, or "No migration required."}
64: ```
65: 
66: Include the spec-folder line only when the release has a spec folder. Add a `## Why This Release` section of 2-4 sentences after the summary only when the summary does not already say why, with an ` ` line before it like every other H2.
67: 
68: ### Expanded Format (10+ changes, major or breaking)
69: 
70: ```markdown
71: {The same frontmatter block as the compact format.}
72: 
73: {Opening narrative: 1-5 paragraphs in plain prose, one per theme, no headers.}
74: 
75: > Spec folder: `{path}` (Level {N})
76: 
77:  
78: 
79: ## Why This Release
80: 
81: {Why the release exists: the gap it closes or the gain it buys, in one to three short paragraphs or bold lead-in gain bullets.}
82: 
83:  
84: 
85: ## What's New at a Glance
86: 
87: - **{The theme, as a short sentence.}** {One plain sentence that adds what the bold one does not say.}
88: 
89:  
90: 
91: ## {Topical Domain}
92: 
93: {Optional 1-2 sentence introduction.}
94: 
95: #### {Benefit-led heading, usually 2-7 words}
96: 
97: {One or two paragraphs for most items, seven at most: what was broken, what changed and why it matters. Start where the glance bullet stopped.}
98: 
99: #### {Next heading}
100: 
101: **Breaking:** {What breaks and exactly what to do about it.}
102: 
103:  
104: 
105: ## Upgrade Notes
106: 
107: - **Adopt.** {Renames and new things to start using.}
108: - **Repoint.** {Moved paths and surfaces that changed address.}
109: - **Drop.** {Removed things and what replaces them.}
110: ```
111: 
112: Include the spec-folder line only when the release has a spec folder.
113: 
114: **Field guidelines**:
115: 
116: - **`{Topical Domain}` (H2).** Name the section for the domain it changes, the way the exemplar names `Spec Kit` and `Safer Git`, never for a change type such as `New Features` or `Bug Fixes`. Most releases need one to five domains. A release the exemplar's size may need more when each one earns its section.
117: - **`{Benefit-led heading}` (H4).** 2-7 words for most headings and 10 at most, stating the gain or the fact. Good: `Specs Move to the Top Level`. Bad: `Improved validation logic`, a numbered item or a sentence-length title.
118: - **Separators.** An ` ` line, a forced blank line, goes before every H2: between the opening and Why This Release, between Why This Release and What's New at a Glance, and between every later section. Nothing separates the H4 items inside one H2, and no `---` rule appears anywhere in the entry body.
119: - **Upgrade Notes.** Use the Adopt, Repoint and Drop lead-ins only when the release has all three kinds of work. Otherwise write plain bullets or a short paragraph, and "No upgrade needed." when there is nothing to do.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 3. WHAT TO LEAVE OUT
124: 
125: What goes in decides the length more than the wording does, so choose the content before writing any of it. Every item dropped stays findable in the spec packet.
126: 
127: ### Choose by Reader Impact
128: 
129: List every change the source records. Keep an item only when the reader would notice it, act on it or decide differently because of it. Merge items that have the same effect for the reader, and lead with the one that matters most. A task list is evidence of what shipped, not an outline: ten tasks that produced one visible change make one bullet.
130: 
131: ### Keep
132: 
133: - User-visible behavior changes, stated as before and after.
134: - Breaking changes and the exact migration step.
135: - Anything the reader must do, adopt, repoint or stop using.
136: - Honest corrections of a claim a previous release got wrong.
137: - Numbers that are the claim itself, such as a measured cost or a limit the reader must stay under.
138: 
139: ### Drop by Default
140: 
141: - File inventories and Files Changed tables.
142: - Test counts, test tables and new test or playbook scenarios.
143: - Schema internals, index churn and machinery names the reader never touches.
144: - Internal labels such as task or requirement IDs, scenario IDs and packet or phase numbers. The spec-folder line is the one pointer an entry needs.
145: - How the work was done: review rounds, models, agents and research phases, unless it changes how far the reader can trust the result.
146: - Follow-on housekeeping: docs brought in line with the change, regenerated copies, rebuilt indexes and refreshed metadata or versions.
147: - Small fixes with no visible effect. Fold several into one sentence, or leave them out.
148: - Work tried and reverted during the cycle. It gets one story sentence at most, written into the narrative: what was tried and that it left before release. The exemplar's model is "An alignment mode was built during the cycle and removed before release, and the removal took `/deep:command-benchmark` and the conformance benchmark family with it."
149: 
150: ### Say Each Fact Once
151: 
152: Each section has one job, and a fact lives in the section whose job it is.
153: 
154: | Section | Its job | Not its job |
155: |---|---|---|
156: | Summary or opening | What the release does, told at the level of themes | Fix-by-fix detail and the numbers behind it |
157: | Why This Release | The gap the release closes or the gain it buys | The list of changes, which the glance section carries |
158: | What's New at a Glance | One line per theme, stating the payoff | The full mechanism or a sentence that restates the bold one |
159: | Topical H4 items | The detail: before, mechanism and after | The glance bullet's sentence, said again |
160: | Upgrade Notes | The actions, one line each | Why the change was made |
161: 
162: When a sentence would repeat an earlier one, cut it or replace it with something the reader does not know yet. In a compact entry, each glance bullet must add something the summary did not say.
163: 
164: ### When a Table Earns Its Place
165: 
166: A table appears only when the numbers are the claim. The exemplar carries one in six hundred lines, the measured cached-input cost per model, because the dollar difference was the finding. A table that restates prose, lists files or counts tests does not earn its place, and most entries carry none.
167: 
168: ### The Cut Test
169: 
170: Before writing the file, ask of each sentence whether the reader would miss it. Cut the ones they would not. Then check the joints: concise is not compressed, so keep the "because" and the before-and-after that make a change make sense, and restore the noun when a cut leaves a "this" with nothing to point at.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 4. WRITING STYLE RULES
175: 
176: These rules apply to changelog files and GitHub release notes. The Human Voice Rules are the authority on banned patterns, and the validator enforces both.
177: 
178: ### Voice
179: 
180: - Write for a smart person who is not a developer.
181: - Lead with why the release matters, never with technical stats.
182: - Explain each change as what was broken, what changed and why it matters.
183: - One idea per sentence, active voice, no hedging.
184: - Define a technical term on first use, such as "BM25 (exact word matching)".
185: - Name an identifier (a skill, a path or a command) only where the reader acts on it, the way the exemplar names `mode-registry.json` where it explains dispatch.
186: - No Oxford commas, em dashes or semicolons, per `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md`.
187: 
188: ### Structure
189: 
190: - Bold lead-in bullets for lists of gains or upgrade steps.
191: - H4 (`####`) for item headings, never H3. No `**Problem:**` or `**Fix:**` labels.
192: - Inline `**Breaking:**` markers where the break is described, not a separate section.
193: - No metrics soup: never pack many numbers into one sentence.
194: 
195: ### Length
196: 
197: | Element | Usually | Ceiling |
198: |---|---|---|
199: | Summary paragraph | 1-2 sentences | 3 sentences |
200: | Expanded opening narrative | 1-3 paragraphs | 5 paragraphs |
201: | Why This Release | 1-2 short paragraphs | 3 short paragraphs or 4 sentences, gain bullets allowed |
202: | What's New at a Glance | 3-6 bullets compact, 5-9 expanded | 12 bullets, one line each |
203: | Glance bullet | A bold sentence and one plain sentence | A bold sentence and three plain sentences |
204: | H4 item narrative | 1-2 paragraphs | 7 paragraphs |
205: | H4 heading | 2-7 words | 10 words |
206: | Compact file total | 10-25 lines of prose | 40 lines of prose |
207: 
208: Validation checks the ceilings, and each one sits at or above what the exemplar does, so the exemplar passes every check it teaches. The usual column is the target. A release with one fix reads short.
209: 
210: ---
211: 
212: ## 5. FORMAT SELECTION GUIDE
213: 
214: | Release Type | Format | When to Use |
215: |---|---|---|
216: | Hotfix (1-3 changes) | Compact | Quick bug fix, typo correction |
217: | Feature release (4-9 changes) | Compact | New feature, small refactor |
218: | Major release (10+ changes) | Expanded | Overhaul, multi-part work |
219: | Breaking change | Expanded | Any release requiring migration, regardless of count |
220: 
221: Count the changes that survive section 3, not the tasks behind them.
222: 
223: ```text
224: Count the changes in the release.
225: ├─> < 10 changes AND not major AND not breaking  → Compact format
226: ├─> >= 10 changes OR major bump                  → Expanded format
227: └─> Any breaking change                          → Expanded format
228: ```
229: 
230: ---
231: 
232: ## 6. GITHUB RELEASE NOTES FORMAT
233: 
234: The release body is the changelog content with any YAML frontmatter and the editorial title H1 removed, because GitHub shows the release title on its own. It keeps the entry's spacing, an ` ` line before every H2 and nothing between H4 items. The release step in the command YAMLs strips both before it runs `gh release create`, then appends an ` ` line and the pointer:
235: 
236: ```text
237:  
238: 
239: Full changelog: `.skilled/changelog/{component}/v{VERSION}.md`
240: ```
241: 
242: The release title is the tag, an em dash and the editorial title, `v{VERSION} — {Editorial Title}`, and the tag is annotated with the message `v{VERSION}: {Editorial Title}`.
243: 
244: ---
245: 
246: ## 7. NESTED PACKET-LOCAL CHANGELOGS (DEPRECATED)
247: 
248: Spec folders no longer get changelogs, so no workflow writes a new file under `specs/**/changelog/`. A change recorded in a spec folder goes into a global entry for the component it touched, written from this template.
249: 
250: Existing `changelog-<packet>-root.md` and `changelog-<packet>-<phase-folder>.md` files stay and still validate. The spec-kit nested generator remains only to render them and prints a deprecation notice. Do not reuse this template for them.
251: 
252: ---
253: 
254: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES
255: 
256: - `.skilled/changelog/skilled/v4.0.0.0.md` - the canonical exemplar this template derives from
257: - [hvr-rules.md](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md) - Human Voice Rules (banned words, punctuation, structure)
258: - [core-standards.md](../../shared/references/core-standards.md) - Markdown structure and naming conventions

260: - [nested-changelog.md](../../../system-spec-kit/references/workflows/nested-changelog.md) - the deprecated nested packet-local changelog workflow

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246: 
247: # Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
248: 
249: Brief introduction (1-2 sentences) explaining what this asset provides and when to use it.
250: 
251: \## 1. OVERVIEW
252: 
253: ### Purpose
254: 
255: [Why this asset exists, what problem it solves]
256: 
257: ### Usage
258: 
259: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: \## 2. SECTION NAME
264: 
265: **Key Points**:
266: - Point 1
267: - Point 2
268: - Point 3
269: 
270: **Template**:
271: ```[language]

273: # With explanatory comments
274: ```
275: 
276: **Field Guidelines**:
277: 
278: **`field_name`**:
279: - Description of field
280: - Format requirements
281: - Example: `value-example`
282:

286: # Ready to copy and adapt

300: 
301: ````

304: 
305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```

711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)

716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point

722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`

743: - Include header row

746: - Use for comparisons or reference data

757: - Every template should have a complete example

762: **Consistency**:

180: # Git Commit Templates

182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187:

189: 
190: ### Usage

193:

201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```

217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343:

346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting

857: ### When to Update Assets

859: **Update asset files when**:
860: - New template variations emerge
861: - User feedback reveals confusion
862: - Standards or conventions change

864: - Examples become outdated
